Notes: Year Established basis: earliest documented Judean presence = the Yahu temple at Elephantine already stood before the Persian conquest. Petition of Yedoniah and the priests to Bagoas governor of Judah (Cowley 30/TAD A4.7; transl. Ginsberg in ANET 491-492): 'our forefathers built this temple in the fortress of Elephantine back in the days of the kingdom of Egypt, and when Cambyses came to Egypt he found it built' (Cambyses' conquest 525 BCE; date = terminus ante quem). Scholars propose an earlier settlement (Sayce/Porten c. 655-650 BCE under Psammetichus I/Manasseh; EJ: temple built 2nd half of 7th or beginning of 6th c. BCE) but these are hypotheses. Presence of an organized community with its own temple; no count.

Sayce (Expositor 8th ser. vol. 2, Aug. 1911) 'The Jewish garrison and temple in Elephantine': states the Yahu temple 'occupied a prominent position in the Jewish quarter'; reports a Hebrew-Aramaic ostracon in his possession (c. 440 BCE) asking a maid be sent 'to prepare the passover'; notes the Berlin papyri call the colony 'the Jewish garrison'. Sayce dates the establishment of the garrison to c. 655 BCE (Letter of Aristeas 13: Jews sent to help Psammetichus against the Ethiopians) and speculates the colony ended in 'massacre or flight' after Egyptian independence (speculation; not documented). Row dated to the ostracon (c. 440 BCE); presence of a garrison community with a Jewish quarter; no count.

Ananiah son of Azariah archive (13 Aramaic papyri 456-402 BCE; Kraeling 1953; TAD B3.1-13; summary by A. Schütze, Trismegistos Archives 2010): Ananiah 'was a servant of the temple of Yahu at Elephantine'; married Tamet (Egyptian slave of Meshullam son of Zakkur) in 449 BCE (B3.3); bought a house at Elephantine in 437 BCE (B3.4); daughter Jehoishma married Ananiah son of Haggai in 420 BCE. Named Jewish individuals/families resident on the island; no count.

Settlement of claim by oath (Cowley 14; ANET 491), dated 14 Ab = 19 Pahons year 25 of Artaxerxes I (440 BCE): the Jewess Mibtahiah daughter of Mahseiah son of Yedoniah, 'an Aramean of Syene of the detachment of Varizata', settles property with the Egyptian builder Pi' of the fortress of Syene. Named Judean individual of the Elephantine-Syene garrison community (Mibtahiah archive); no count.

Encyclopaedia Judaica (Schalit/Matassa), 'Elephantine': 'The Elephantine Jews constituted a military unit known as "the Jewish force"'; every Jewish soldier belonged to a degel (company/regiment); a smaller unit called 'a hundred' also attested; 'There were also Jews at Elephantine who were not part of the military establishment', besides soldiers' families. Dated to the Persian period (539-332 BCE midpoint -435; documents cover 5th c. BCE). Organized military colony with families; no total given.

'Passover Papyrus' (Cowley 21/TAD A4.1), year 5 of Darius II = 419 BCE: letter of Hananiah 'To my brothers, Yedaniah and his colleagues the Jewish garrison' instructing observance of the Festival of Unleavened Bread in Nisan by royal authority. Attests the organized Jewish garrison community and its leader Yedaniah; no count.

Event: destruction of the Yahu temple. Petition to Bagoas (Cowley 30; ANET 492): in Tammuz, year 14 of Darius II (410 BCE), while the satrap Arsames was away, the priests of Khnub conspired with Vidaranag, who ordered his son Nefayan, commander of the garrison of Syene, to destroy 'the temple of the god Yaho in the fortress of Yeb'; Egyptians and other troops razed it, burnt its cedar roof and looted its gold and silver vessels. The community fasted in sackcloth 'we and our wives and our children'. The community itself remained.

Petition (Cowley 30/TAD A4.7), dated 20 Marheshwan year 17 of Darius II = 25 Nov. 407 BCE: 'To our lord Bagavahya governor of Judah, your servants Jedaniah and his colleagues the priests who are in Elephantine the fortress', requesting permission to rebuild the temple destroyed in 410 BCE; earlier letters to the high priest Johanan in Jerusalem unanswered. Attests a functioning priestly community with wives and children; no count.

Petition probably to Arsames (Cowley 33; ANET 492), undated, c. 407 BCE (c.; follows the memorandum of Bagoas and Delaiah authorizing rebuilding with meal-offering and incense only): five named men 'Syenians who hold property in the fortress of Elephantine' (Yedoniah son of Gemariah, Ma'uzi son of Nathan, Shemaiah son of Haggai, Hosea son of Yatom, Hosea son of Nathun) offer payment and 1000 ardabs of barley if the temple is rebuilt without animal sacrifice. 5 = petitioners only (subset), not the population.

Ananiah archive (Schütze, Trismegistos 2010): in 402 BCE Ananiah son of Azariah and Tamet sold remaining parts of their Elephantine house to their son-in-law Ananiah son of Haggai (B3.12); the document mentions the temple of YHW, which 'was apparently rebuilt when the document was written'. Last document of the archive is a loan of Ananiah son of Haggai, 402 BCE (B3.13). Continued Jewish residence and rebuilt temple; no count.

Collection list for the cult of Yaho (Cowley 22/TAD C3.15; ANET 491), dated 3 Phamenoth year 5 (of Amyrtaeus = c. 400 BCE, or of Darius II = 419 BCE per ANET n.7): 'the names of the Jewish garrison which gave money to the God Yaho, 2 shekels each'; ANET: lines 2-119, 126-135 'name 123 contributors of both sexes'; cash with Yedoniah son of Gemariah 31 karash 8 shekels (12 k. 6 sh. for Yaho, 7 k. for Ishumbethel, 12 k. for Anathbethel). 123 = donors on one list (men and women; subset), so Population left blank; it suggests a community of at least several hundred persons including children, but no source gives a total.

Encyclopaedia Judaica (Schalit/Matassa): 'the account of the community in the papyri ends in 399 b.c.e.' (latest documents dated to Amyrtaeus year 5 and the accession of Nepherites I); it is not certain whether the Jewish colony at Elephantine persisted after the end of Persian rule. End of documentation; not a documented absence, so Population blank (not 0).

Wikipedia, 'Elephantine papyri and ostraca' (last-resort source): 'By the middle of the 4th century BCE, the temple at Elephantine had ceased to function.' c. mid-4th c. BCE. Event: end of the Yahu temple; no source found documenting Jews at Elephantine/Syene in the Ptolemaic or early Roman periods. Population blank.
